cards.statement: The GitHub UI offers Run workflow for a workflow file that is on a feature branch and absent from the default branch.
cards.explanation: The Run workflow button appears when the workflow file is on the default branch. After a first run, the REST API or GitHub CLI can dispatch it against another branch or tag.
cards.misconception: Choosing a feature branch in the UI lifts the default-branch requirement for the Run workflow button.

cards.statement: A boolean workflow_dispatch input becomes a string in the inputs context.
cards.explanation: The inputs context preserves a workflow_dispatch boolean as a Boolean. github.event.inputs represents that value as a string.
cards.misconception: Both dispatch input contexts stringify boolean values.

cards.statement: repository_dispatch types filters match the event_type value sent by an API caller.
cards.explanation: The caller supplies event_type when creating a repository_dispatch event; the workflow's types list selects which values trigger it.

cards.statement: The branches filter on pull_request matches the pull request's head branch.
cards.explanation: For pull_request, branches filters the branch the pull request targets. The source branch is available through github.head_ref.
cards.misconception: The pull_request branches filter checks the contributor's source branch.

cards.statement: pull_request_target reads its workflow file from the repository's default branch.
cards.explanation: The workflow source for pull_request_target is the default branch even when the pull request targets another base branch.
cards.volatilityNote: GitHub changed this security-sensitive ref behavior in December 2025.

source.title: Actions pull_request_target and environment branch protections changes

cards.statement: A push trigger with branches and paths filters runs when both filters match.
cards.explanation: GitHub combines a push branch filter and path filter with AND; a matching branch alone does not trigger the workflow.

cards.statement: A workflow_run completed trigger waits for the preceding workflow to succeed.
cards.explanation: workflow_run with the completed activity starts after the named workflow completes regardless of its conclusion.
cards.misconception: The completed activity means the earlier workflow succeeded.

cards.statement: secrets: inherit passes secrets to a called workflow in another organization of the same enterprise.
cards.explanation: inherit passes every secret the caller can reach, including organization, repository and environment secrets, to a called workflow in the same organization or enterprise.

cards.statement: workflow_call accepts environment as a declared input type.
cards.explanation: A workflow_call input declares boolean, number, or string. environment is an input type for workflow_dispatch.
cards.misconception: Manual and reusable workflow triggers accept the same input types.

cards.statement: A job that needs a failed job still runs when its own if condition uses always().
cards.explanation: A failed or skipped needs dependency normally skips the dependent job; always() in jobs.<job_id>.if lets it run regardless of that result.

cards.statement: A job-level if expression can read matrix.os for each generated matrix child.
cards.explanation: GitHub evaluates jobs.<job_id>.if before applying strategy.matrix, so matrix values are unavailable to that condition.
cards.misconception: Job-level if is evaluated separately after each matrix child is generated.

cards.statement: A step's env value overrides a same-named job env value while that step runs.
cards.explanation: For a variable defined at several workflow levels, the most specific value applies during that step.

cards.statement: After ::stop-commands::TOKEN, the runner ignores workflow commands until a step echoes ::TOKEN::.
cards.explanation: stop-commands pauses workflow command processing so a step can print text such as a script without running it as commands; echoing the same unique token resumes processing.

cards.statement: A service container's options key accepts Docker's --network flag.
cards.explanation: jobs.<job_id>.services.<service_id>.options accepts Docker container options, but GitHub explicitly excludes --network.
cards.misconception: Every Docker create option is usable for a workflow service container.

cards.statement: A job running in a container needs a host port mapping to reach its service container.
cards.explanation: A container job reaches its service through the service label on their shared Docker network. Host port mapping is needed when the job runs directly on the runner.
cards.misconception: Container jobs use the same service port mapping as jobs running on the host.

cards.statement: A matrix include entry that conflicts with an original axis value overwrites that original combination.
cards.explanation: include adds its keys to every combination it does not conflict with; only an entry that fits no combination becomes a new one. Original matrix values are never overwritten.
cards.misconception: An include entry replaces an original matrix variant when its axis value conflicts.

cards.statement: With strategy.max-parallel unset, GitHub runs as many matrix jobs at once as runners allow.
cards.explanation: GitHub maximizes parallel matrix jobs based on available runners; strategy.max-parallel caps how many of a matrix's jobs run at the same time.

cards.statement: A YAML alias can reuse an entire anchored job configuration elsewhere in one workflow file.
cards.explanation: GitHub Docs show an anchor on a job mapping and an alias that supplies that mapping to another job in the same file.

cards.statement: A step that writes to GITHUB_ENV reads the new value during that same step.
cards.explanation: Writing to GITHUB_ENV makes the value available to subsequent steps in the same job, not to the step writing it.
cards.misconception: GITHUB_ENV updates the current process environment immediately.

cards.statement: A step that writes to GITHUB_OUTPUT exposes its value through steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
cards.explanation: GITHUB_OUTPUT sets a named output for the current step; later steps refer to it using that step's id.

cards.statement: A dependent job reads a needed job's declared outputs through the jobs.<job_id>.outputs context.
cards.explanation: A job that lists another job in needs reads that job's declared outputs through needs.<job_id>.outputs.<output_name>.
cards.misconception: The jobs context exposes job outputs to dependent jobs in any workflow.

cards.statement: A reusable workflow output maps to an output from one of its jobs.
cards.explanation: on.workflow_call.outputs declares the workflow output and sets its value from a job-level output inside the called workflow.

cards.statement: Appending Markdown to GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY places it in the job log.
cards.explanation: Markdown written to GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY appears in the job summary on the workflow run summary page.
cards.misconception: The summary file appends its content to ordinary step logs.

cards.statement: actions/cache tries restore-keys in order after failing to match its primary key.
cards.explanation: The cache action checks its primary key first, then checks supplied restore-keys sequentially for a usable match.

cards.statement: Omitting name in actions/download-artifact fetches all of the run's artifacts, one folder per artifact.
cards.explanation: Omitting name makes the action download all artifacts uploaded in the current workflow run, creating a directory named after each artifact.

source.title: Store and share data with workflow artifacts

cards.statement: actions/upload-artifact retention-days overrides an organization retention maximum.
cards.explanation: An artifact's retention-days value cannot exceed the repository, organization, or enterprise retention limit.
cards.misconception: Per-artifact retention can exceed an administrator's configured ceiling.

source.title: Store and share data with workflow artifacts

cards.statement: GitHub assigns an environment job to a runner before its protection rules pass.
cards.explanation: GitHub sends a job that references an environment to a runner after its deployment protection rules pass.
cards.misconception: Environment protection happens after runner allocation.

cards.statement: For an open pull_request run, GITHUB_REF points to the contributor's head branch.
cards.explanation: For an unmerged pull_request run, GITHUB_REF identifies the pull request's merge ref, such as refs/pull/42/merge.
cards.misconception: The pull_request execution ref is the contributor's source branch.

cards.statement: A matrix include entry restores a job combination that the same matrix's exclude list had removed.
cards.explanation: GitHub processes all include combinations after exclude, so an include entry that matches an excluded combination adds that job back to the matrix.

cards.statement: A two-version, two-OS matrix with exclude: [{os: windows-latest}] removes one job.
cards.explanation: An exclude entry may match just one axis. Excluding windows-latest removes both Windows variants in a two-version matrix.
cards.misconception: A partial matrix exclusion removes a single generated combination.

cards.statement: A failing matrix job set to continue-on-error: true makes fail-fast cancel its sibling jobs.
cards.explanation: A matrix job with continue-on-error: true can fail while the other matrix jobs keep running; fail-fast cancels in-progress and queued jobs when a job with continue-on-error: false fails.
cards.misconception: fail-fast cancels the matrix whenever any job fails, whatever its continue-on-error setting.

cards.statement: For a failed step using continue-on-error, steps.<id>.outcome reads success.
cards.explanation: A failed step's outcome remains failure; continue-on-error changes its final conclusion to success.
cards.misconception: continue-on-error rewrites the step's raw outcome.

cards.statement: A workflow rerun keeps the GITHUB_SHA from the original triggering event.
cards.explanation: Rerunning a workflow uses the original event's commit SHA rather than the branch's newer tip.

cards.statement: A matrix job can be rerun individually with gh run rerun --job JOB_ID.
cards.explanation: GitHub CLI accepts a specific job ID for a rerun, so a failed matrix variant can be selected.

cards.statement: A job skipped by a job-level if condition reports Success to required checks.
cards.explanation: GitHub reports a skipped conditional job as Success, so that required check does not block a pull request merge.

source.title: Using conditions to control job execution

cards.statement: A job's system.txt log shows expanded values for its job-level if condition.
cards.explanation: The job's system.txt includes the original if expression, context values substituted into it, and the evaluation result.

cards.statement: The workflow runs REST API accepts an event filter to narrow run history.
cards.explanation: The list workflow runs endpoint accepts event as a query parameter, such as push or pull_request.

source.title: REST API endpoints for workflow runs

cards.statement: A log archive from a partial rerun includes jobs from previous attempts.
cards.explanation: A partial rerun's log archive contains the rerun jobs. Download earlier attempts' archives to collect logs for the other jobs.
cards.misconception: The latest archive combines logs from all attempts.

cards.statement: ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG adds runner process logs to the downloaded archive.
cards.explanation: ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG increases step-log verbosity. Runner process logs belong to runner diagnostic logging.
cards.misconception: Step debugging and runner diagnostics produce the same log files.

cards.statement: Viewing a public repository's workflow runs requires a GitHub sign-in.
cards.explanation: Even for public repositories, GitHub shows workflow run information, such as run status and logs, only to people logged in to a GitHub account.

cards.statement: actions/download-artifact needs a token and run ID to fetch another run's artifact.
cards.explanation: Artifacts from a different workflow or workflow run are fetched by supplying a token and the run identifier to the download-artifact action.

source.title: Store and share data with workflow artifacts

cards.statement: The artifacts REST API reports each artifact's expires_at timestamp.
cards.explanation: Artifact metadata returned by the REST API includes expires_at, which identifies its scheduled expiration time.

source.title: REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions artifacts

cards.statement: The artifact download REST endpoint returns ZIP bytes directly.
cards.explanation: The endpoint returns a redirect to a temporary URL for the artifact ZIP archive.
cards.misconception: The initial artifact API response is the archive itself.

source.title: REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions artifacts

cards.statement: Deleting a workflow run leaves its uploaded artifacts available for download.
cards.explanation: Deleting a workflow run also removes every artifact associated with that run from storage.
cards.misconception: Run deletion and artifact deletion are independent.

cards.statement: The workflow log search includes messages from collapsed steps.
cards.explanation: GitHub's workflow log search searches expanded steps, so expand a step before searching its messages.
cards.misconception: The log search indexes collapsed and expanded step output alike.
cards.volatilityNote: This depends on the current workflow-log UI search behavior.

cards.statement: Editing an organization workflow template leaves workflows already created from it unchanged.
cards.explanation: Choosing a template commits a copy of it as a new workflow file in the repository. For logic that should update centrally, the template can call a reusable workflow.

cards.statement: Organization workflow templates live in `.github/workflows` of the organization’s `.github` repository.
cards.explanation: Organization templates go in the `workflow-templates` directory of the organization’s `.github` repository.
cards.misconception: Workflow templates use the same directory as runnable workflows.

source.title: Creating workflow templates for your organization

cards.statement: A workflow template defines its chooser description in the workflow YAML file.
cards.explanation: A same-name `.properties.json` file supplies the workflow template’s displayed name and description.
cards.misconception: The template YAML supplies its chooser description.

source.title: Creating workflow templates for your organization

cards.statement: An internal `.github` repository offers its workflow templates to public repositories in the enterprise.
cards.explanation: Templates from an internal .github repository are offered only to internal and private repositories. Only a public .github repository serves templates to every repository type.
cards.misconception: Internal workflow templates are offered to public repositories.

cards.statement: GitHub automatically replaces `$default-branch` in a template when a repository creates a workflow from it.
cards.explanation: At creation time, GitHub substitutes the target repository’s default branch name for `$default-branch`.

source.title: Creating workflow templates for your organization

cards.statement: A template’s `filePatterns` regex matches files anywhere in a repository tree.
cards.explanation: A template is eligible when `filePatterns` matches a file in the repository root.
cards.misconception: Template file patterns scan the full directory tree.

cards.statement: A reusable workflow’s release tag takes precedence over a branch with the same ref name.
cards.explanation: For `{owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{file}@{ref}`, GitHub resolves a same-named release tag before a branch.

cards.statement: A composite action can choose a runner that differs from its caller job’s runner.
cards.explanation: A composite action runs as a step in the caller job; a reusable workflow can define jobs with their own runners.
cards.misconception: Composite actions select their own job runner.

cards.statement: GitHub disables the scheduled workflows in a new fork of a public repository.
cards.explanation: When a public repository is forked, its scheduled workflows start disabled to prevent unneeded runs; the fork owner can enable them again from the Actions tab.

cards.statement: For JavaScript actions, `runs.using: node24` selects the current GitHub Actions runtime.
cards.explanation: GitHub’s current JavaScript action runtime is Node.js 24, selected through the action’s `runs.using` metadata.
cards.volatilityNote: GitHub retired Node.js 20 in September 2026; action runtimes can change.

source.title: Node 20 is no longer available in GitHub Actions

cards.statement: A Docker container action can execute on a Windows self-hosted runner that has Docker installed.
cards.explanation: Docker container actions execute on Linux runners; a self-hosted Linux runner also needs Docker installed.
cards.misconception: Installing Docker makes Windows self-hosted runners eligible for container actions.

cards.statement: Composite action `runs.steps` accepts both `run` commands and `uses` steps.
cards.explanation: The composite action’s step list can call other actions as well as execute shell commands.

cards.statement: A downloaded JavaScript action requires an `npm install` step before its `runs.main` executes.
cards.explanation: A JavaScript action is downloaded as a complete package; its required dependencies must be included or bundled for distribution.
cards.misconception: The workflow must install downloaded action packages before execution.

cards.statement: A local JavaScript action can use `runs.pre` to prepare its `runs.main` execution.
cards.explanation: The `runs.pre` script runs before `main` for supported JavaScript actions, but GitHub does not support it for local actions.
cards.misconception: Local JavaScript actions support the pre hook.

cards.statement: In a job that sets jobs.<job_id>.container, a JavaScript action step runs inside that job container.
cards.explanation: jobs.<job_id>.container runs every step that names no container of its own inside the job container, so JavaScript actions execute there and not on the host.

cards.statement: A Docker container action whose Dockerfile switches to a non-root USER loses access to GITHUB_WORKSPACE.
cards.explanation: Docker container actions must run as the default Docker user, root; a USER instruction in the Dockerfile cuts the action off from the GITHUB_WORKSPACE directory.

cards.statement: A `uses: ./.github/actions/build` step reads the action from GitHub before `actions/checkout` runs.
cards.explanation: A `./` action path resolves in the runner workspace, so the repository must be checked out before that step.
cards.misconception: A relative action path downloads directly from the repository.

cards.statement: A Docker action’s `runs.entrypoint` is ignored when its Dockerfile declares `ENTRYPOINT`.
cards.explanation: The action metadata’s `runs.entrypoint` overrides the Dockerfile `ENTRYPOINT` instruction.
cards.misconception: Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT takes priority over action metadata.

cards.statement: GitHub reads a custom action's metadata from `action.yaml` as well as `action.yml`.
cards.explanation: A custom action uses `action.yml` or `action.yaml`; GitHub prefers `action.yml`.

cards.statement: A composite action's run steps read caller inputs from INPUT_<NAME> environment variables.
cards.explanation: GitHub creates no INPUT_<NAME> variables for composite actions; their steps read caller values through the inputs context, for example ${{ inputs.name }}.
cards.misconception: Composite actions receive inputs as INPUT_ environment variables like JavaScript and Docker actions.

cards.statement: GitHub rejects an action call automatically when an input marked `required: true` is omitted.
cards.explanation: For custom actions, `required: true` does not automatically produce an error when the caller omits the input.
cards.misconception: The required metadata flag is enforced by the runner.

cards.statement: The `outputs.<id>.value` key maps a composite action output to one of its own step outputs.
cards.explanation: Composite action metadata can expose a nested step output through an expression in `outputs.<id>.value`.

cards.statement: A JavaScript action's post script runs after a later job step fails when post-if is unset.
cards.explanation: post-if defaults to always(), and its status check functions read the job's status, so the action's cleanup runs even when later steps fail.

cards.statement: A composite action inherits the caller job’s default shell for each `run` step.
cards.explanation: A composite action step with `run` requires an explicit `shell` field in the action metadata.
cards.misconception: Composite run steps inherit the workflow shell setting.

cards.statement: In a JavaScript action, `core.setSecret` masks a value in later workflow log output.
cards.explanation: The Actions toolkit’s `core.setSecret` maps to `add-mask`, which redacts the registered value from subsequent log lines.

cards.statement: In a JavaScript action, `core.saveState` publishes a value for a downstream job.
cards.explanation: `core.saveState` uses `GITHUB_STATE` to pass state within the same action’s lifecycle, including its post script.
cards.misconception: Saved action state is a cross-job output.

cards.statement: An action’s `branding` metadata controls the icon and color shown beside its Marketplace name.
cards.explanation: GitHub Marketplace displays the action badge using its metadata `branding.icon` and `branding.color` values.

cards.statement: GitHub Marketplace requires a published action to reside in a public repository.
cards.explanation: Marketplace publishing requires the action repository to be public and to contain action metadata at its root.

cards.statement: An action’s Marketplace display name comes from its GitHub release title.
cards.explanation: GitHub Marketplace uses the `name` in the action’s metadata file for the action listing.
cards.misconception: Release titles determine the action listing name.

cards.statement: Two Marketplace actions can share a metadata `name` when their repository owners differ.
cards.explanation: The action metadata `name` must be unique among published GitHub Marketplace actions.
cards.misconception: Marketplace names are unique only within each owner.

cards.statement: Pushing a version tag to an action repository lists the action in GitHub Marketplace.
cards.explanation: Maintainers publish an action in Marketplace by creating and publishing a release with the Marketplace option selected.
cards.misconception: Tag creation alone publishes an action listing.

cards.statement: A repository owner’s Verified profile badge also gives its action a Marketplace verified creator badge.
cards.explanation: GitHub treats the profile Verified badge and Marketplace verified creator badge as different credentials.
cards.misconception: Profile verification grants Marketplace creator verification.

cards.statement: Action maintainers can move a major version tag to the Git ref of a newer compatible release.
cards.explanation: Updating a floating tag such as `v1` lets callers follow newer compatible action releases.

cards.statement: Enabling release immutability on an action repository locks the assets of releases published before it was enabled.
cards.explanation: Release immutability applies only to releases published after the setting is enabled; releases published earlier stay editable.
cards.misconception: Turning on immutability retroactively locks existing releases.

cards.statement: Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem also bumps refs of reusable workflows called in workflows.
cards.explanation: With package-ecosystem "github-actions", Dependabot keeps both action references and reusable workflows used inside workflows up to date, opening pull requests for outdated refs.

source.title: Keeping your actions up to date with Dependabot

cards.statement: An enterprise Actions policy can enable GitHub Actions for selected organizations.
cards.explanation: Enterprise owners can enable Actions for every organization, selected organizations, or none.

source.title: Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise

cards.statement: An organization allowlist identifies a reusable workflow with `OWNER/REPO@REF` syntax.
cards.explanation: Allowed reusable workflow patterns include the owner, repository, workflow path, filename, and ref.
cards.misconception: An action reference pattern also identifies a reusable workflow.

source.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

cards.statement: An organization can require action references to use full-length commit SHAs.
cards.explanation: The organization policy applies to actions, including GitHub-authored actions; reusable workflows can still use tags.

source.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

cards.statement: The “Allow actions created by GitHub” setting admits Marketplace actions from verified creators.
cards.explanation: GitHub-owned actions and Marketplace actions by verified creators have separate allow settings.
cards.misconception: The GitHub-owned option includes all verified creators.

source.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

cards.statement: An organization can require approval before public-fork pull request workflows from first-time contributors run.
cards.explanation: The organization’s fork approval setting can hold these workflow runs for approval by a user with repository write access.

source.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

cards.statement: A caller repository’s Actions access setting opens a private reusable workflow in another repository.
cards.explanation: The repository that stores the private reusable workflow sets its Access policy to admit callers.
cards.misconception: The caller sets the source repository’s sharing access.

source.title: Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository

cards.statement: The “Run workflows from fork pull requests” policy sends secrets into private-fork workflow runs.
cards.explanation: That policy runs private-fork pull request workflows with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no secrets; sending secrets has its own policy.
cards.misconception: Running private-fork workflows also enables secrets.

source.title: Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization

cards.statement: Users need Read access to a private or internal `.github` repository to use its workflow templates.
cards.explanation: For nonpublic organization templates, the organization grants Read access to the users or teams that should use them.

cards.statement: An organization’s allowed-action list blocks a `uses: ./...` action that lacks an allowlist entry.
cards.explanation: Allowed-action policies do not restrict local actions loaded from the runner filesystem through `./` paths.
cards.misconception: Allowed-action patterns restrict checked-out local actions.

source.title: Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise

cards.statement: GitHub routes a self-hosted job by runner group even when its `runs-on` labels differ.
cards.explanation: GitHub routes a self-hosted job to an online, idle runner matching the job’s group and labels.
cards.misconception: A matching runner group overrides mismatched labels.

cards.statement: A runner group restricts which repositories send jobs to its self-hosted members.
cards.explanation: Runner group access policies control which repositories may use self-hosted or larger runners.

cards.statement: An ephemeral self-hosted runner returns to the idle pool after finishing a job.
cards.explanation: GitHub assigns one job to an ephemeral self-hosted runner and deregisters it after that job.
cards.misconception: Ephemeral runners remain registered for more work.

cards.statement: ARC's runner scale set listener learns about queued jobs through an HTTPS long-poll connection to GitHub.
cards.explanation: The listener pod authenticates to the GitHub Actions Service and holds an HTTPS long poll open until a Job Available message arrives, then scales the runners up.

cards.statement: An enterprise using an IP allow list can run its Actions jobs on standard GitHub-hosted runners.
cards.explanation: With an IP allow list, Actions needs self-hosted runners or GitHub-hosted larger runners with static IP ranges, and admins add those runners' addresses to the allow list.
cards.misconception: Standard hosted runners pass an enterprise IP allow list like any other GitHub traffic.

source.title: Restricting network traffic to your enterprise with an IP allow list

cards.statement: The `actions` field of `GET /meta` reports IP ranges used by GitHub-hosted runners.
cards.explanation: GitHub’s REST meta endpoint publishes hosted runner address ranges; the ranges change over time.

cards.statement: A past job’s `Included Software` link lists today’s tools for its runner label.
cards.explanation: The `Set up job` log links to the tool list for the specific runner image that executed that job.
cards.misconception: Old job logs link to the current runner image tool list.

cards.statement: A self-hosted runner writes job execution diagnostics to `Runner_` files in `_diag`.
cards.explanation: `Worker_` files in `_diag` contain per-job logs; `Runner_` files record the runner application’s activity.
cards.misconception: Runner_ files are the per-job diagnostic logs.

cards.statement: Self-hosted runners update their runner application automatically by default.
cards.explanation: Registration with `--disableupdate` turns off automatic software updates, leaving admins to update the runner.

cards.statement: On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, `gh secret set --org` defaults an organization secret to private repositories.
cards.explanation: GitHub CLI defaults an organization secret to private-repository visibility unless its access options change.

cards.statement: A repository’s Actions secrets page lists organization secrets granted to that repository.
cards.explanation: Repository settings show accessible organization secrets alongside the repository’s own Actions secrets.

cards.statement: An environment secret reaches sibling jobs that omit the matching `environment` key in the same workflow.
cards.explanation: Environment secrets reach jobs that reference their environment; other jobs in the workflow do not receive them.
cards.misconception: One environment job shares its secrets with sibling jobs.

cards.statement: A repository secret wins over an environment secret with the same name in an environment job.
cards.explanation: For a job using an environment, the environment-level secret takes precedence over same-named repository and organization secrets.
cards.misconception: Repository secrets outrank environment secrets on a name collision.

cards.statement: A reusable workflow's `vars` context reads the caller repository's variables.
cards.explanation: A called workflow sees the configuration variables of the caller's repository; variables in the repository that stores the reusable workflow are not passed in.

cards.statement: GitHub resolves an environment-level variable while evaluating the workflow’s `run-name`.
cards.explanation: Environment-level configuration variables become available after the job starts on a runner, too late for workflow-level `run-name`.
cards.misconception: Environment variables are available while GitHub sets the run name.

cards.statement: A reference to an unset `secrets` entry evaluates to `null` in a workflow expression.
cards.explanation: An unset secret reference such as `${{ secrets.KEY }}` evaluates to an empty string.
cards.misconception: Absent secrets resolve to null.

cards.statement: The Actions Secrets REST API returns a repository public key for encrypting secret values before upload.
cards.explanation: The repository public-key endpoint supplies the key and key ID needed to submit an encrypted secret.

source.title: REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions Secrets

cards.statement: The Actions Variables REST API updates a repository variable through `PUT`.
cards.explanation: Repository variable updates use `PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/variables/{name}`.
cards.misconception: Repository variable updates use PUT.

source.title: REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions variables

cards.statement: A job-level `permissions` map adds scopes to the workflow-level `GITHUB_TOKEN` grants.
cards.explanation: Job-level `permissions` set that job’s token scopes; permissions omitted from an explicit map become `none`.
cards.misconception: Job permissions extend the workflow permission map.

cards.statement: A self-hosted job’s `GITHUB_TOKEN` can expire while that job is still running.
cards.explanation: The token has an effective maximum lifetime that can end before a long self-hosted job finishes.
cards.volatilityNote: Token renewal policy for long self-hosted jobs may change.

cards.statement: A job with `id-token: write` gains write access to its repository.
cards.explanation: `id-token: write` permits requesting an OIDC JWT; it does not grant write access to repository contents.
cards.misconception: OIDC token permission also grants repository write access.

cards.statement: Renaming a repository after July 15, 2026 leaves its OIDC `sub` claim in the name-only format.
cards.explanation: Repositories created, renamed or transferred after July 15, 2026 use the immutable sub format with owner and repository IDs, such as repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:...
cards.misconception: Only newly created repositories switch to the immutable subject format.

cards.statement: GitHub inserts `${{ }}` values into a `run` script before the shell runs, enabling script injection.
cards.explanation: Expression values are pasted into the generated shell script, so an untrusted PR title can run as commands. Pass it through an intermediate env variable instead.

cards.statement: One approval from a listed reviewer satisfies an environment's required-reviewer rule.
cards.explanation: Only one of the listed users or teams has to approve; with Prevent self-review on, the user who started the deployment cannot be that approver. Other protection rules, such as a wait timer, still apply.

cards.statement: An environment's deployment branches and tags rule controls which users may approve its deployment jobs.
cards.explanation: Deployment branches and tags restrict which branches or tags can deploy to the environment; approvers come from the required reviewers rule.
cards.misconception: The deployment branches rule doubles as an approval list.

cards.statement: A full-length commit SHA is GitHub’s recommended pin for a third-party action in a secure workflow.
cards.explanation: A full commit SHA ties the action reference to a specific revision rather than a movable tag.

cards.statement: `gh attestation verify` checks a binary's attestation against the repository given with `-R`.
cards.explanation: GitHub CLI uses the artifact path and `-R OWNER/REPO` to verify the artifact attestation against its source repository.

source.title: Using artifact attestations to establish provenance for builds

cards.statement: The `cache: npm` input of `actions/setup-node` caches the Node.js runtime selected by `node-version`.
cards.explanation: The `cache` input caches npm package-manager data; `node-version` selects the Node.js runtime separately.
cards.misconception: The setup-node npm cache stores the Node.js runtime.

cards.statement: GitHub bills a repository's extra cache storage only after its cache storage limit is set above the included allowance.
cards.explanation: Each repository has an included cache allowance; GitHub charges for cache usage beyond it only when the repository's cache storage limit is configured higher than that allowance.

cards.statement: Shorter artifact retention reduces accrued artifact storage usage in a private repository.
cards.explanation: GitHub accrues Actions artifact storage usage over time, so artifacts deleted earlier stop adding future usage.
cards.volatilityNote: GitHub Actions storage billing rules may change.

cards.statement: With the default queue setting, a new run in a concurrency group cancels the run pending there.
cards.explanation: A concurrency group holds one pending run by default, so the newer run replaces it. queue: max lets runs wait instead, and cancel-in-progress also cancels the running one.

source.title: Control the concurrency of workflows and jobs

cards.statement: A re-run of a failed private-repository workflow on GitHub-hosted runners adds its minutes to the failed attempt's.
cards.explanation: Minutes a failed attempt used stay counted: a workflow that fails after 5 minutes and then succeeds in a 10-minute re-run uses 15 minutes of the owner's allowance.

cards.statement: A run's log files and job summary count toward the repository owner's artifact storage allowance.
cards.explanation: Logs and job summaries do not count as artifact storage; uploaded artifacts do, and they share one storage allowance with GitHub Packages.
cards.misconception: Everything a workflow run stores is billed as artifact storage.

cards.statement: In a private repository, parallel hosted jobs share one billable runtime total while they overlap.
cards.explanation: GitHub measures runner time per job, so parallel jobs accrue their own execution minutes.
cards.misconception: Overlapping jobs are billed as one elapsed interval.

cards.statement: GitHub provides self-hosted runner execution free of GitHub Actions minute charges.
cards.explanation: GitHub does not charge Actions runner minutes for self-hosted jobs, though you still operate the machines.
cards.volatilityNote: GitHub Actions billing rules may change.

cards.statement: In private repos, larger runners spend included standard minutes before billing starts.
cards.explanation: GitHub bills larger runner execution separately from included standard runner minutes, including for public repositories.
cards.misconception: Included standard minutes offset larger-runner usage.
